title: Health vs. Disease Concepts

sections.learningObjectives:
- Distinguish health, wellness, and disease.
- Contrast acute and chronic disease and signs versus symptoms.
- Describe levels of prevention (primary, secondary, tertiary).
- Differentiate modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors.
- Apply health-versus-disease concepts to communication, documentation, and screening in the medical office.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of health like a garden: it is not just free of weeds (disease); it also needs good soil, sun, and water (body, mind, and relationships) to really thrive.

### Question 2

Being healthy is like a three-legged stool: the body, the mind, and your friendships all have to hold you up. If one leg is missing, the stool wobbles even if the others are fine.

### Question 3

Wellness is like practicing a sport: you keep training and making good choices over time, not just winning one game.

### Question 4

Wellness is like a pizza with many slices: being active, feeling calm, having friends, and keeping your brain busy are all different slices of the same pie.

### Question 5

Disease is when a part of the body stops working the way it should, like a machine with a broken part.

### Question 6

Disease is what the doctor can measure; illness is how you feel on the inside, like the difference between a thermometer reading and feeling hot and miserable.

### Question 7

Homeostasis is like a thermostat: the room temperature goes up and down a little, but the heater and air conditioner keep it in a comfortable range.

### Question 8

Your body is like a car that keeps its engine temperature steady whether it is hot or cold outside; when that system fails, the car (or body) gets into trouble.

### Question 9

Pathophysiology is like studying how a machine breaks down and what the broken parts do to the whole machine.

### Question 10

Etiology is the 'why did this happen' question, like finding out who started a leak in the roof.

### Question 11

Idiopathic is a fancy word for 'we do not yet know the reason,' like a mystery with no identified culprit.

### Question 12

A syndrome is like a recipe: several ingredients (signs and symptoms) that show up together tell you what dish you are looking at.

### Question 13

Prognosis is the weather forecast for a disease: how it is expected to go and whether it will clear up, linger, or worsen.

### Question 14

Diagnosis is like a detective naming the culprit after gathering all the clues from the patient and the tests.

### Question 15

A person can wear glasses and still be healthy and active; the glasses manage a problem so the person can live fully.

### Question 16

Health and disease are like 'full' and 'hungry': different states on a scale, not two words for the same thing.

### Question 17

A sign is something you can see or measure from the outside, like a rash or a high temperature on a thermometer.

### Question 18

A symptom is something only you can feel inside, like a headache; nobody else can see it.

### Question 19

Only the patient knows how dizzy they feel, so dizziness is a symptom they share with you.

### Question 20

The thermometer shows the number, so a fever is a sign anyone can read, like the speed on a car's speedometer.

### Question 21

Nausea is like an upset stomach only you can feel; a bruise is something everyone can see.

### Question 22

A rash is like a stain on a shirt that everyone can see; a headache is something only the person feels.

### Question 23

Vital signs are like the dashboard gauges in a car: numbers anyone can read to check how the machine is running.

### Question 24

It is like a car that both makes a strange noise (symptom) and has a visibly flat tire (sign); both clues matter.

### Question 25

One is what the person tells you they feel; the other is a number you count yourself. Both go in the record, but in different columns.

### Question 26

It is like separating facts you saw yourself from things someone told you; keeping them straight avoids confusion.

### Question 27

A back ache is something only the patient can feel and tell you about, so it is a symptom.

### Question 28

Swelling is something you can see or measure, like water pooling where it should not be; tiredness only the patient feels.

### Question 29

A sign is something you can point to; a symptom is something the patient has to tell you about.

### Question 30

It is like a friend who feels cold while the thermometer shows a normal room; you write down both what they feel and what the thermometer says.

### Question 31

Only the patient can feel the throbbing, so it is a symptom they share with the team.

### Question 32

Acute is like a sudden rainstorm: it comes on fast and passes quickly.

### Question 33

Chronic is like a slow, steady leak that needs regular attention over a long time.

### Question 34

An ear infection is like a quick storm that blows over; diabetes is like a long, slow season.

### Question 35

Diabetes is like caring for a garden all season long, not just watering it once.

### Question 36

The flu is like a fast-moving storm that arrives quickly and then leaves.

### Question 37

High blood pressure is like a slow leak that needs watching over years, not a one-day fix.

### Question 38

An exacerbation is like a fire that usually smolders suddenly flaring up and needing quick attention.

### Question 39

Remission is like calm weather between storms, when a condition quiets down for a while.

### Question 40

It is like a car that has always had a small engine problem suddenly sputtering badly; the old problem just got worse fast.

### Question 41

Acute is a sprint; chronic is a marathon. One is quick and intense, the other long and steady.

### Question 42

Calling it chronic is like saying a plant needs water every week, not just one time.

### Question 43

A broken bone from one fall is like a sudden crack in a window, not a slow change.

### Question 44

Osteoarthritis is like slow wear on a hinge over many years, not a sudden break.

### Question 45

Subacute is like medium-sized: not a quick flash and not a forever thing, but somewhere in between.

### Question 46

Three days and sudden is like a sprinter, not a long-distance runner; that is an acute picture.

### Question 47

A risk factor is like driving in the rain: it makes a skid more likely, but it does not mean you will definitely skid.

### Question 48

It is like a cloudy sky: rain is more likely, but it might still stay dry.

### Question 49

Things you can choose to change, like what you eat or whether you exercise, are the knobs you can turn.

### Question 50

Some things, like your birthday or your family tree, are fixed; you cannot rewrite them.

### Question 51

You cannot change who is in your family, so family history is a fixed risk marker.

### Question 52

Tobacco use is a habit someone can decide to change, like a switch they can flip.

### Question 53

You can choose to move more, but you cannot choose your relatives; so the lifestyle part is the one you can change.

### Question 54

It is like checking the weather before a trip so you know whether to pack an umbrella.

### Question 55

A risk factor is like adding weight to one side of a scale; it tips the odds but does not force the outcome.

### Question 56

It is like carrying both an umbrella and a raincoat in a storm: together they change your chances more than either alone.

### Question 57

Helping someone quit smoking is a change the patient and office can work on together, unlike changing a birthday.

### Question 58

Primary prevention is like wearing a helmet before you ever fall, so the injury never happens.

### Question 59

Secondary prevention is like a smoke detector that finds a problem early, before the whole house is in flames.

### Question 60

Tertiary prevention is like repairing and strengthening a roof after a storm so the damage does not get worse.

### Question 61

A vaccine is like building a shield before the battle starts, so you never get hurt.

### Question 62

A mammogram is like a camera that catches a small problem early, when it is easier to handle.

### Question 63

Cardiac rehab is like physical training after an injury so the person regains strength and avoids more problems.

### Question 64

Teaching healthy habits is like teaching someone to swim before they ever go near deep water.

### Question 65

A blood pressure station is like a checkpoint that catches a problem early so it can be handled.

### Question 66

Physical therapy is like rebuilding strength after an injury so life can get back on track.

### Question 67

A seatbelt is like putting a gate at the top of the stairs so no one ever falls.

### Question 68

A Pap test is like checking a roof for small leaks before they become big holes.

### Question 69

Prevention is like caring for a house at every stage: keeping it dry, catching leaks early, and repairing damage.

### Question 70

Checking a person's feet regularly is like inspecting a dam for cracks before it breaks.

### Question 71

Washing hands is like cleaning up a spill before anyone slips; it stops the problem before it starts.

### Question 72

A cholesterol test is like checking the oil in a car before the engine shows any trouble.

### Question 73

It is the order of a story: stop trouble before it starts, catch it early, then fix what is already broken.

### Question 74

The patient is telling their side of the story; the assistant writes it down so the doctor hears it too.

### Question 75

If you see smoke, you tell someone right away; visible trouble should never wait.

### Question 76

A report like this is like a fire alarm going off; you do not wait to see if it stops, you call for help.

### Question 77

Screening is like checking a smoke detector's battery even when there is no smoke, so you are ready before trouble.

### Question 78

Family history is a question about your family tree, which you cannot change; the other questions are about habits you can.

### Question 79

Habits like smoking or drinking are choices that can be changed, unlike your birthday or family history.

### Question 80

It is like reporting both the noise a car is making and the warning light on the dash; both clues help the mechanic.

### Question 81

Screening is like a yearly check under the hood even when the car runs fine, to catch problems early.

### Question 82

It is like scheduling a tune-up for an older car to keep small issues from becoming breakdowns.

### Question 83

It is like teaching someone good habits today so they stay out of trouble tomorrow.

### Question 84

Sudden one-sided weakness is a red flag; the assistant's job is to sound the alarm and hand it to the experts, not to solve it.

### Question 85

Write down both what the patient tells you and what you measure, like keeping two tidy columns in a notebook.
